newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Flagship bank CA sold to Bank Austria.
newsitem.headline: Flagship bank CA sold to Bank Austria.

text.p: Almost 141 years after it was founded by the Rothschild family, Austria's flagship bank Creditanstalt-Bankverein on Sunday fell under the control of newcomer Bank Austria.
Set up to finance the development of Europe's railway network under Austro-Hungarian imperial rule, the bank has turned into one of the most powerful players in Austria's modern-day business life.
The bank's ups and downs run like a thread through the often-troubled history of Austria and the Danube empire from which the small Alpine nation emerged 80 years ago.
On the eve of the First World War, Creditanstalt already held stakes in some 100 of the empire's biggest industrial concerns, located in Prague, Pilzen or Trieste.

Most of those holdings were lost when the empire broke up, and the ensuing hyperinflation of the 1920s almost wiped out what had at the turn of the century become one of Europe's biggest financing houses.
Losses piled up, and by the spring of 1931, the bank informed the government it was teetering on the brink of insolvency. The ensuing run on the bank almost wiped it out.

By 1934, the bank had sold most of its remaining industrial holdings and more than half of its equity was taken over by the state. Four years later, Creditanstalt fell under German control when Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany.
Closed in 1944, the bank started from scratch in 1945, helping to finance Austria's reconstruction from the rubble that the country was reduced to during the final years of World War Two.
Today, hundreds of the nation's top industrial concerns still rely on Creditanstalt for their long-term financing.

The bank directly or indirectly controls a sizeable chunk of Austria's industry. The list of the bank's equity holdings includes brick maker Wienerberger Baustoffindustrie K and fibre-maker Lenzing, both of which are part of the blue-chip ATX index of 21 shares, and car maker Steyr-Daimler-Puch.
Creditanstalt's influence on the Vienna bourse, one of Europe's oldest but smallest, is no less significant. The bank accounts for more than a third of trading.

Its own stock is among the 10 most actively traded issues on the stock exchange. Both its ordinary shares, 70 percent of which were held by the republic, and its widely held preference stock are part of the blue-chip ATX index.

Closely allied with conservative industrialists, Creditanstalt was firmly in the camp of the rightist People's Party and one of the most obvious examples of Austria's system of "proporz" whereby economic might is divided along party lines.

Social Democrat-controlled Bank Austria's bid for the conservative bank had put Creditanstalt's management on the defensive. One source close to the board said the takeover was nothing but a "Soviet-style privatisation".

Chief executive Guido-Schmidt Chiari, who has run the bank since 1988, had been equally hostile. "This is my bank," he told enraged employees when thousands of the bank's 9,700 staff turned out to protest against expected job losses.
The battle was lost on Sunday when Chancellor Franz Vranitzky announced that the bank had gone to the highest bidder -- Bank Austria.

Creditanstalt's total assets stood at 689 billion schillings ($62.13 billion) at the end of last year. Net profit was at 2.6 billion schillings ($234.4 million), up from 2.166 billion a year ago. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
